newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: BRAND RETURN MAY HERALD NEW AD INDUSTRY GOLDEN AGE.
newsitem.headline: BRAND RETURN MAY HERALD NEW AD INDUSTRY GOLDEN AGE.

text.p: Focus on building brandnames to swell a client's bottom line could return the advertising industry to the "Golden Age of Creativity" it enjoyed in the 1960s, top advertising agency executives said on Tuesday.
Speaking at the Financial Mail's International Advertising Conference 1997, executives said the industry also needed to redefine brands and advertising's role in promoting them.
The golden age of creative advertising stretched from the late 1950s to the early 1970s -- a time when advertising played an unprecedented role in driving company and product profits.

As it heads into the next century, the advertising industry must develop a model which challenges a market's status quo and focuses on maximising success rather than minimising failure, said Burt Manning, chairman of J.Walter Thompson Co Worldwide.

"(This) will lead to more big, huge brand successes and a better return on a client's investment and may lead to a return to the Golden Age of Creativity," said Manning whose agency carries names like Kellogg , Kodak and Rolex.
"I am seeing some very encouraging signs. There is a renewed and intense focus on building brands. We do not make or sell products. We make and sell brands," he added.

Manning cited sportswear giant Nike and Absolut Vodka as examples of clients willing to risk being creative in their advertising campaigns and currently enjoying the financial fruits of their courage and foresight.

What constitutes a brand must also be redefined and broadened to allow more scope for creativity, said Derek Carstens, chief executive officer of South Africa's biggest advertising agency Ogilvy & Mather Rightford (Pty) Ltd.

"Brands are too narrowly defined and are therefore restricting the advertising involvement. Brands are business tools used to create wealth for our clients. The Golden Age of Creativity will re-emerge because the tools are becoming more sophisticated," Carstens said.

He called for a holistic and multi-dimensional approach to advertising which would allow a bigger canvas for creativity and allow relationships between advertising, sales, consumers, profits and share price to be developed to their fullest.
In addition to the product and its quality, the brand should include the company's mission, its culture and its role in the wider social and economic sphere, Carstens said.
He quoted David Ogilvy, founder of Ogilvy & Mather:
"A brand is a complex symbol. It is the intangible sum of a product's attributes."
